# Acknowledgments {.unnumbered}

This book grew out of the Speak Software programming labs: twelve core labs, each built around a real client brief, plus three staff-tool labs that turn this book's harness chapters into tools a department of one keeps. The labs came first and supplied the spine. Every lab kills one misconception and installs one habit, and the chapters here add the why, the guardrails, and the management layer the labs deliberately leave out.

Thanks are due to the students and testers who worked through the labs while they were still rough. A brief that looked clear on the page and fell apart in the room got rewritten. A check nobody ran got cut or automated. The slop gate, the evidence-trio linter, and the lab doctor in this book's `tools/` folder exist because lab work showed where unaided confidence failed.

Several public arguments anchor the book and are credited where they are used. Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code at Anthropic, supplied the answer to the slop question and the mini-CEO framing: prototypes can be black boxes, production code written by AI gets a higher bar, met with guardrails. Jake Van Clief and David McDermott's Interpretable Context Methodology supplied the folders-over-agents framing: one capable agent reading the right files at the right moment, instead of a framework of specialised agents. Anthropic's Agent Skills documentation supplied the concrete skill-folder pattern the book implements. Andrej Karpathy named vibe coding. The author's *Conversation, Not Delegation* (2025) supplied the Conversation Loop and the VET framework this book builds on.

The open-source community behind Quarto, Pandoc, Python, and GitHub made it possible to write, check, and publish this book, its tools, and the companion labs from text files the reader can inspect. The manuscript checks, the slop gate, and the trio linter all run on that stack.

This book was written using the method it prescribes. AI agents drafted, summarised, proposed structures, and built tooling at every stage, under specification and check. They also produced fluent errors on schedule, which is why the book insists that a guarded pipeline, not confidence, is the verdict. The machine made the work faster. The judgement, and the responsibility for every claim that remains, are the author's.
